records.title: Sowing into planting pits
records.summary: Build pits before the rains, fill them with soil and organic matter, and sow a few seeds into each once the rains are reliable.
instructions: Dig pits in the softest spots, about a forearm wide and as close to a forearm deep as the hard layer allows.
Pile dug soil on the downhill side as a small lip to catch runoff.
Fill with dug soil mixed with one to two bucketfuls of compost or manure, plus leaf litter or chopped grass.
Leave the filled surface a little below ground level so the pit catches water.
Wait for reliable rains, then sow in the centre of each pit: a pinch of four or five millet seeds about one finger-joint deep, or two or three bean-sized seeds about two finger-joints deep.
When seedlings have a few leaves, thin to the strongest two or three (millets) or one or two (legumes).
Mulch around seedlings once they are up.
everyday_amounts: pits about a forearm wide and deep (where possible)
about a long pace between pits
one to two bucketfuls of compost per pit
a few seeds per pit, about one finger-joint deep
limitations: Shallow pits on hard ground can fill with water; give them an overflow notch if water stood in the drainage check.
safety_notes: Do not force tools through rock; keep away from edges; mark open pits.

records.title: Sowing into knee-high raised beds
records.summary: Build beds upward over the hard layer, let the first rain settle them, and sow in rows or spots across the bed.
instructions: Edge a bed about one arm-span wide with stones, logs or packed earth.
Fill in layers: scraped soil, compost or manure, leaf litter and grass, finishing about knee-high.
Let the first good rain settle the bed; top up any low spots.
Sow in short rows across the bed or in spots about a hand-span apart for small millets, wider for legumes.
Mulch between rows once seedlings are up.
Where water pools, keep the paths between beds open so water drains away.
everyday_amounts: beds about knee-high and one arm-span wide
spots about a hand-span apart for millets, about a forearm apart for legumes
a few seeds per spot, about one finger-joint deep
limitations: Beds dry faster than the ground in dry spells; mulch heavily.
safety_notes: Do not strip soil from slopes or edges to fill beds.

records.title: Growing in containers or sacks
records.summary: On a continuous rock sheet, grow a few plants in filled sacks, containers or stone rings.
instructions: Use sacks, broken containers or stone rings about a forearm across, with drainage gaps at the bottom.
Fill with a mix of scraped soil and organic matter.
Sow a few seeds per container after reliable rains; thin to one or two strong plants.
Mulch the top and keep close to stored water.
everyday_amounts: containers about knee-high when filled
one or two plants per container
limitations: Only a few plants; a trial or stop-gap.
safety_notes: Never use containers that held fuel, poisons or chemicals.

records.title: Laying stone lines across the slope
records.summary: Lay stones along the contour, a few paces apart, before the rains; plant along the uphill side where soil and moisture collect.
instructions: Find the slope direction (pour-water check or watching the first rain).
Mark level lines across the slope a few paces apart.
Scrape a shallow groove and set large stones downhill with smaller stones packed behind.
Check where overflow will go; it must end somewhere safe.
Plant pits, beds or grass and hedge cuttings just uphill of the lines.
Repair after every heavy rain.
everyday_amounts: lines about ankle to shin high
a few paces apart
limitations: Lines that are not level make water run along them and break through.
safety_notes: Never send runoff toward homes, paths, neighbours or edges.
Lift stones carefully.

records.title: Planting in half-moon catchments
records.summary: On gentle slopes, plant crops or a young tree inside half-moon basins that open uphill.
instructions: Build half-moons a couple of paces across, open side uphill, bank lined with stones.
Mix compost or organic matter into the lower part of the basin.
Sow a few seeds or plant a tree seedling in the lower part, where water gathers.
Mulch the basin floor; repair the bank after storms.
everyday_amounts: a couple of paces across
a bucketful or two of compost per basin
limitations: Not for flat pooling ground or steep slopes.
safety_notes: Never point overflow toward homes or paths.

records.title: Confirm the rains are reliable before sowing
records.summary: Wait until soaking rains have come more than once and the soil is moist down to the hard layer before sowing most of your seed.
instructions: Count the soaking rains since the season started; one shower is not enough.
The day after a rain, dig with a stick beside a pit: the soil should be moist all the way to the hard layer.
Ask neighbours whether this is when rains usually settle in.
If unsure, sow only part of the seed now and keep the rest to re-sow.
everyday_amounts: more than one soaking rain
soil moist down to the hard layer
limitations: Even reliable-looking rains can pause; keep reserve seed and stored water.

records.title: Sowing seeds: depth, spacing and thinning
records.summary: Sow a few seeds per spot into moist pits or beds: small seeds about one finger-joint deep, bean-sized seeds about two finger-joints deep, then thin to the strongest plants.
instructions: Sow in the early morning or late afternoon into soil that is moist down to the hard layer.

Depth: tiny seeds (niger, little millet) are only just covered; small seeds (finger millet, pearl millet) about one finger-joint deep; bean-sized seeds (cowpea, horse gram, groundnut, pigeon pea) about two finger-joints deep.
Seeds per spot: a small pinch of four or five millet seeds; two or three bean-sized seeds; one or two shelled groundnuts.
Spacing in beds: millets about a hand-span apart each way; legumes about two hand-spans apart; rows across the bed, not along a slope.
Spacing in pits: sow in the centre of each pit, in the lowest part where water collects; pits themselves about a long pace apart.
Cover the seed, press the soil gently with your palm so seed touches moist soil, and mark the spot with a small stick.
Keep back a handful of each seed for re-sowing gaps.
Thinning: when seedlings have three or four leaves, keep the strongest two or three millet plants or one or two legume plants per spot; pinch out (do not pull) the rest to avoid disturbing roots.
Write what you sowed, where and when in the journal.
everyday_amounts: small seeds about one finger-joint deep; bean-sized seeds about two finger-joints deep; tiny seeds just covered
a pinch of four or five millet seeds, or two or three bean-sized seeds, per spot
millets a hand-span apart, legumes two hand-spans apart in beds; pits a long pace apart
thin to two or three millet plants or one or two legume plants per spot
keep back a handful of each seed for re-sowing
limitations: Seeds sown too deep in crusting soil may not come up; seeds sown too shallow dry out.
Spacing is a starting point: on very poor soil, wider spacing shares scarce water better.
safety_notes: Wash hands after handling any treated seed; never eat treated seed.

records.title: Mulching after sowing
records.summary: Once seedlings are up, spread mulch around them and keep it topped up through dry spells.
instructions: Wait until seedlings are visible, then spread mulch around them, leaving a finger's width clear of each stem.
Keep a layer about a hand's depth when fresh, thicker before a dry spell.
Top up as termites and weather break it down.
everyday_amounts: a layer about a hand's depth when fresh
an armful per pit
limitations: Mulch can shelter pests; check under it now and then.
safety_notes: Check grass for snakes before gathering.

records.title: Harvesting and storing rainwater
records.summary: Catch rain from roofs, sheets or tarps into covered containers, and use it only to rescue seedlings in dry spells.
instructions: Set clean, covered containers under a roof edge, sheet or tarp before storms.
Let the first minutes of rain rinse the surface before collecting.
Keep containers covered and shaded.
In a dry spell, give each seedling a cupful at the base, early morning or evening.
Refill whenever it rains.
everyday_amounts: a cupful per seedling in dry spells
limitations: Stored water is small; it rescues seedlings, it does not irrigate a field.
safety_notes: Never use containers that held fuel or chemicals; keep drinking water separate; cover containers.

records.title: Planting tree seedlings in enlarged pits
records.summary: Plant tree seedlings or cuttings at the start of reliable rains in the deepest pocket you can find, in a pit enlarged as much as the ground allows and filled with good soil.
instructions: Use your probing marks to find the deepest pocket or a crack in the hard layer.
Before the rains, enlarge the pit as wide and deep as the ground allows without forcing rock (aim for wider than a forearm).
Fill with topsoil mixed with compost or manure and leaf litter.
At the start of reliable rains, plant the seedling at the same depth it grew in its pot or bag; firm the soil.
Build a small basin or half-moon around it and mulch widely.
Help it with stored water in the first dry season; shade it with a few branches if needed.
Protect from grazing animals with thorny branches.
everyday_amounts: pit wider than a forearm, as deep as the ground allows
two or more bucketfuls of compost per tree pit
limitations: On a continuous rock sheet, trees will struggle; plant only in cracks or pockets.
safety_notes: Do not force tools through rock.
Keep pits marked so people do not fall in.

records.title: Re-sowing gaps after a dry gap or failed germination
records.summary: If seedlings die in a dry gap or fail to come up, re-sow the empty spots with reserved seed as soon as the soil is moist again.
instructions: A week or so after sowing, count spots with no seedlings.
If rain has returned and the soil is moist to the hard layer, re-sow those spots with reserved seed.
If time is short, re-sow with the quickest crop you have (such as pearl millet, little millet or cowpea).
everyday_amounts: the handful of seed you kept back
limitations: Re-sowing uses up part of the season; this is why the plan adds buffer weeks.

records.when_to_sow: As soon as the soil is moist again after a failed start.

records.title: Mixing millet and legume
records.summary: Sow millet and a legume (cowpea or horse gram) in alternate pits or rows to share risk and feed the soil.
instructions: Alternate millet and legume pits, or sow rows of each across a bed.
Do not crowd: thin each crop to its usual number per spot.
Next season, swap places.
everyday_amounts: alternate pits or rows
limitations: Mixed crops compete for scarce water in dry spells; keep spacing generous.

records.when_to_sow: After the first reliable soaking rains: more than one good rain, soil moist down to the hard layer, and no long dry gap expected. Not after a single shower.

records.title: Buried unglazed clay pot
records.summary: Bury an unglazed clay pot up to its neck beside one or a few plants and keep it filled; water seeps slowly through the clay to the roots with little lost to the sun.
instructions: Use an unglazed, unpainted clay pot with a narrow neck (glazed or painted pots do not seep).
Before sowing, bury it in a pit or bed up to its neck, so the mouth sits just above the soil.
Sow or plant two to four plants around it, about a hand's width from the pot wall.
Fill the pot with stored water and cover the mouth with a flat stone or lid to stop evaporation and mosquitoes.
Check every few days with a finger: refill when the pot is about half empty.
Test before relying on it: fill it and feel whether the soil beside it is damp by the next day.
everyday_amounts: one pot per pit or a few plants
plants about a hand's width from the pot
refill when about half empty
limitations: Pots crack if they dry out and refill in strong sun; keep them partly full.
Seepage is slow in tight soil and fast in gravel; watch and adjust.
Only as much area as you can keep the pots filled from stored water.
safety_notes: Cover the pot so children, animals and mosquitoes cannot get in.
Never use containers that held fuel, poisons or chemicals.
Keep drinking water separate and covered.

records.title: Bottle drip from a household bottle
records.summary: Make a slow drip from a plastic bottle with a tiny hole in its cap, buried neck-down beside a plant, to deliver stored water straight to the roots.
instructions: Make one or two tiny holes in the bottle cap with a hot nail or thorn; the water should drip, not pour.
Cut the bottom off the bottle (or make a hole) so it can be refilled.
Push the bottle neck-down into the soil about a hand's width from the plant, cap buried about a finger-joint deep.
Fill it with stored water in the cool of the morning or evening and cover the open end with a leaf or cloth.
Check that the soil around the cap gets damp; widen the hole if nothing comes out, narrow it if it empties at once.
everyday_amounts: one bottle per plant or per seedling pit
a hand's width from the stem
limitations: Holes clog with soil; check and clear them.
Only for a few plants; it is a rescue measure.
safety_notes: Handle hot nails with care.
Never use containers that held fuel, poisons or chemicals.
Keep drinking water separate and covered.

records.title: Mulched basin around each plant
records.summary: Shape a small saucer-shaped basin around each plant or pit, keep it mulched, and pour water only into the basin so none runs off.
instructions: Scrape a shallow saucer about a forearm across around the plant, with a low ring of soil on the edge.
Fill the basin with mulch, keeping a finger's width clear of the stem.
When watering, pour slowly into the basin, under the mulch, so it soaks in rather than running away.
Rebuild the ring after heavy rain.
everyday_amounts: a basin about a forearm across
mulch about a hand's depth
limitations: On pooling ground, basins can hold too much water after storms: open the ring on the downhill side in heavy rain.
safety_notes: Never send overflow toward homes or paths.

records.when_to_sow: At sowing or transplanting, and kept through the season.

records.title: Watering at the base in the cool of the day
records.summary: Give stored water at the base of the plant, under the mulch, only in the early morning or evening.
instructions: Water only when the soil a finger deep under the mulch is dry, not on a fixed schedule.
Pour slowly at the base or into the basin, never over the leaves.
Use a cup or a can with small holes so water soaks in rather than running off.
Water early morning or late afternoon; midday water evaporates.

check a finger deep before watering
limitations: Watering every day wastes stored water and keeps roots shallow.

records.title: Matching planted area to stored water
records.summary: Use stored water for seedlings and flowering plants first, and never plant more spots than your stored water can rescue through a dry spell.
instructions: Before sowing, count stored buckets and the number of planting spots: plan on rescuing every spot through at least one dry gap.
Water order in a dry spell: newly sown and seedling spots first, then flowering plants, then the rest.
If water runs low, keep the best pits alive rather than spreading water thinly over all.
Expand the planted area only when storage has grown, not before.

seedlings first, then flowering plants
limitations: A long dry spell can exhaust any household store; mulch and timing matter more than watering.

records.title: Soil mixes for pits, beds, tree pockets and greens
records.summary: Fill every planting pocket with clean soil mixed through with mature compost, a thin plain-soil top and mulch, adjusted for pits, raised beds, tree pockets and small greens beds.
instructions: Where to find fill soil: fine soil gathered behind stone lines, soil from gaps between stones, dry stream-bed silt, old abandoned termite-mound soil and rotted leaf litter. Leave stony crumbs out.
Planting pit: stop at the solid hard layer; widen rather than force. Mix soil and mature compost all through the rooting layer, top with a thin layer of plain soil, then mulch.
Raised bed: build a stable stone border, fill with the same soil-and-compost mix, top with plain soil and mulch, and give it an overflow notch.
Tree pocket: use whatever depth the workable soil allows, widen or build up instead of forcing a deep hole, mix compost through the root zone, and shape a low basin only where water drains.
Greens patch: a container with drainage holes or a small rich bed of soil and plenty of mature compost, near shelter and clean water.
If you try ash or crushed shell at all, keep it to a small, well-mixed trial patch, away from seed and roots.
Do the squeeze test on the mix: it should hold together loosely and crumble when poked.
everyday_amounts: roughly half soil and half mature compost by bucketfuls in the richest pits
a thin layer of plain soil on top
mulch about a hand's depth
limitations: Do not plant in a pocket where water stays standing.
Do not rely on a thick layer of dry grass at the bottom to hold water; mix organic matter through.
safety_notes: Take mound soil only from old, empty termite mounds.
Do not use silt or soil that smells of fuel or chemicals, or lies below rubbish.

records.when_to_sow: Mix and fill before the first reliable rains, so the fill settles before sowing.

records.title: Planting cuttings, tops and slips
records.summary: Plant sweet potato vines, cassava stems, pineapple tops, moringa cuttings and grass-hedge slips once the soil is well wet, with the right part buried and the growing tip out.
instructions: Sweet potato: take vine tips about a forearm long from healthy plants; bury a few leaf joints at a slant in a mound or raised bed with the tip out.
Cassava: cut stem pieces about a forearm long from healthy plants; push about two-thirds into a tall mound at a slant with buds pointing up.
Pineapple: twist off the leafy top, let the cut end dry for a few days, then set it into a rich pit or bed just deep enough to stand firm.
Moringa and gliricidia: push thick cuttings about a forearm long a hand deep into a filled pit, or along stone lines for a live hedge.
Grass hedge: split clumps into slips and plant them about a hand-span apart in a tight line on the uphill side of a stone line.
Firm the soil, mulch around (not over) the cuttings, and keep them damp for the first couple of weeks.
everyday_amounts: cuttings about a forearm long
slips about a hand-span apart in a line
about two-thirds of a cassava stem buried
limitations: Cuttings from diseased plants spread disease.
Cuttings dry out fast in sun: plant the same day they are cut, in the cool of the day.
safety_notes: Use a sharp knife carefully.
Cassava stems and leaves are not food without proper processing.

records.title: Finding seed when you have none
records.summary: If no seed is on hand, look for planting material in the kitchen, from fruit, from neighbours and from wild plants, and test it before sowing.
instructions: Kitchen and market: dry cowpeas or other beans, raw (unroasted) groundnuts, whole millet or sorghum grain.
From food: sweet potato pieces or vine tips, a pineapple top, seeds from chilli or squash fruit.
From people: ask neighbours, local farmers, markets or a farm extension office for a handful of locally adapted seed.

records.title: Covered rainwater store in a natural hollow (with strong safety limits)
records.summary: Where the hard layer forms a natural hollow that holds rain, it can be used as a separate, covered water store for base-watering, never as a planting pit, and only where it is safe.
instructions: Use only a shallow, natural hollow on stable ground, well away from edges, drop-offs, homes and paths.
Keep it separate from planting pits: crop roots must never stand in it.
Cover it securely with branches and a sheet, or a lid, so children and animals cannot fall in and mosquitoes cannot breed.
Make a safe overflow so a full store spills to stable ground.
Draw water with a container for careful base-watering only; do not drink it unless it is properly made safe.
everyday_amounts: a shallow hollow only
covered at all times
limitations: Open water evaporates fast in the dry season and is quickly fouled.
If there is any doubt about safety, use covered household containers instead.
safety_notes: Drowning risk: never make or keep a deep or uncovered water hole; keep children and animals away.
Mosquitoes breed in open water within days: keep it covered; empty or fill in a store you cannot keep covered.
Keep well away from edges and unstable ground.
Do not use if the water looks oily, smells of chemicals or receives runoff from rubbish.
